data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories inevitably smuggles induction back into Popper's system because any decision to act on a theory (e.g., building a bridge based on physics) implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past regarding the theory's validity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one can demonstrate a purely logical or evolutionary imperative to prefer survivors without assuming future resemblance, the induction charge fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'action' can be decoupled from 'expectation of success' (e.g., acting simply to test), the pragmatic need for induction vanishes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Exposing the pragmatic contradiction: Popper forbids inferring 'true' from 'survived tests,' yet his own advice to 'prefer' the survivor for action entails an implicit premise that survival predicts future reliability. Without this inductive bridge, 'preference' is arbitrary.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
